references.text: Moses tells the people that the Lord will give them meat to eat in the evening and bread to satisfy them in the morning, as a test to see whether they will follow the Lord's law or not.

In the evening, quails come and cover the camp, and in the morning there is dew around the camp. When the dew disappears, something fine and flake-like lies on the ground, which the Israelites do not recognize. Moses explains that this is the bread the Lord has given them to eat.
The Israelites call the bread manna. It is white like coriander seed and tastes like cakes made with honey.

Moses reminds the Israelites how the Lord provided for them in the wilderness, where they ate manna, something their ancestors did not know, to teach them that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of the Lord.

The psalm tells how God commanded the clouds from above and opened the doors of heaven to rain down manna for his people to eat, and gave them grain from heaven. Thus man ate the food of angels; He sent them food in abundance.

It invites those who are thirsty to come to the waters, and those who have no money: Come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without cost. Ask why they spend money on what is not bread, and their labor on what does not satisfy.
Jesus answers the devil during the temptation in the wilderness by saying it is written: 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.'
A parallel account to the event in Matthew 14:17, where the disciples also report here that they have only five loaves and two fish before Jesus feeds five thousand men.
A parallel account where Jesus feeds five thousand men with five barley loaves and two fish, as a sign of his divine provision.
A parallel account to the event in Matthew 14:17, where Jesus feeds four thousand men with seven loaves and a few small fish, emphasizing the importance of understanding the miracles he performs.
